A1.justification: Both PDFs describe RubricRL and contain readable main texts, equations, tables, figures, and supplementary material. Original experiments and visual examples can be matched despite extensive reformatting and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original text-to-image RL experiments on GenEval and DPG-Bench, including sampling, normalization, grader, and rollout-budget ablations.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original diffusion-model evaluations, human studies, aesthetic measurements, and further ablations.

M1.justification: v2 adds an implemented diffusion branch using DiffusionNFT, including velocity-space optimization and an EMA sampling policy (Section 3 and Appendix A.4). v1 implements only AR training with GRPO. The shared binary rubric reward and original AR sampling procedure remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Training retains JourneyDB and Synthetic-1M, and generation evaluation retains GenEval and DPG-Bench. Additional backbones, aesthetic scoring, and human judging do not establish new generation-task or prompt-domain coverage; no distinct new dataset or input scenario is identified.

E2.justification: Appendix B.1 adds continuous-score rubric supervision as an evaluated alternative to the proposed binary supervision. The external reward comparator set remains CLIPScore, HPSv2, Unified Reward, LLaVA-Reward-Phi, AR-GRPO, and X-Omni; the earlier sampling and grader comparison sets are retained.

E3.justification: New diffusion experiments introduce Qwen-Image and FLUX configurations, LoRA training, and diffusion-specific sampling settings. v2 also adds CLIP+MLP aesthetic evaluation and human protocols covering preference, rubric validity, and grader agreement, including 1,000 prompt–rubric pairs and ten annotators. Previously specified AR training settings are retained.

E4.justification: New analyses test binary versus continuous feedback, rubric counts of 4/8/10/12, aesthetic quality alongside compositional accuracy, and human agreement with rubrics and graders. Appendix D adds cost and convergence analysis. Earlier sampling, normalization, Best-of-N, counting-failure, grader, and rollout-budget analyses remain.

E5.justification: v2 newly displays error bars for human preference and judge agreement in Figure 5 and discusses lower variance. Their definition and estimation procedure are unspecified. Neither version reports training seeds or repeated-training-run counts, so additional training repetitions cannot be inferred.

E6.justification: All 32 original main benchmark rows retain their values. New diffusion results include RubricRL GenEval scores of 0.9091 for Qwen-Image and 0.8969 for FLUX (Table 3). New human results report 98.1% rubric consistency and 94.8% grader agreement; additional ablation, aesthetic, and cost results substantially expand the evidence.

T1.justification: Appendix A.4 adds mathematical specifications for DiffusionNFT's bounded optimality probability, positive/negative velocity mixtures, regression objective, and EMA update. This formalizes the added optimizer; the original rubric, GRPO, and sampling mathematics is retained, with no new theorem, proof, or theoretical guarantee.

C1.justification: The central architecture-agnostic, interpretable rubric-reward contribution remains. The introduction refines the control contribution from a general user-controllable interface to developer-controlled rubric categories adjusted through system-prompt edits. The abstract now explicitly describes validation on both AR and diffusion models.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations for binary feedback benefiting discrete correctness, excessive rubrics introducing redundancy, and aesthetic gains arising from decomposed supervision. Appendix D discusses API cost, accessibility, and difficulties distilling general-purpose graders. These substantially extend v1's retained counting-failure and sampling/grader tradeoff discussions.

D1.justification: v2 supplies all three prompting templates, including rubric-selection priorities, diffusion hyperparameters and EMA details, human-study instructions/interfaces, rubric caching, and runtime/API-cost information. It also newly specifies AR CFG scale 7.5 and DPG prompt rewriting; these disclosures do not establish changes to the earlier AR experiments.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to FLUX, DiffusionNFT, and the CLIP+MLP aesthetic predictor, while removing T2I-R1. DiffusionNFT enters the discussion of diffusion RL. The broader positioning against composite and unified rewards, and the rubric-reward novelty claim, remain substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained. Local rewrites clarify AR/diffusion branches and developer control, related work gains numbered subsections, normalization variants are renamed, and supplementary material is organized into Sections A–E. This is not a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column layout, redraws Figures 2–3, and restructures benchmark tables. New displays include diffusion and ablation tables, a human-study plot, prompt-template panels, and annotation screenshots. Earlier qualitative grids are largely retained and renumbered.

improvement.justification: v1 claimed architecture independence while testing only AR models and lacked direct rubric-reliability validation. v2 substantially addresses these gaps through diffusion comparisons, human studies, and targeted design ablations, while full prompts and optimizer details improve reproducibility. Undefined human-study error bars and appendix editing inconsistencies limit reporting quality, but do not outweigh the stronger support for the central contribution.
